# Notes on 1 Corinthians 15:1–29

**What I couldn't find:** My searches didn't turn up anything from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, oca.org, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or the Pentecostal sites (pneumareview.com, samstorms.org, ag.org). I also found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this passage. Those parts are missing below. Two pages, Enduring Word and Bible Hub's v. 22 page, cut off partway through, so I only have Guzik's notes up to about v. 5. My search results gave me nothing usable for vv. 8–10.

---

**v. 1–2**
- Guzik says the gospel only helps people if they receive it and stand in it. Even with all their faults, the Corinthians were still standing in it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/
- On "hold firmly": Guzik says they had to keep holding on to the gospel. If someone lets go, their earlier belief does them no good, as if they had believed in vain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

**v. 3**
- Guzik says Paul didn't invent this gospel. He received it and passed it on. The core of it is real events in history, not advice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/
- On "for our sins": Guzik says God the Father laid on the Son the guilt and wrath our sin deserved, and Jesus fully satisfied that wrath in our place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/
- Catholic view (catholic.com): Verses 3–7 are treated as a very early creed. The speaker cites Gerd Lüdemann, who rejects the resurrection, as dating its elements to "the first two years after the crucifixion of Jesus." https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/the-creed-written-days-after-jesus-rose

**v. 4**
- Guzik on the burial: it proves Jesus really died, and it fulfils Isaiah 53:9. He calls the cross the payment and the empty tomb the receipt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/
- On "the third day": Guzik says Jewish counting treated part of a day as a whole day, so 72 full hours aren't needed. For "according to the Scriptures" he points to Hosea 6:2, Jonah 1:17 and Psalm 16:10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

**v. 5**
- Ellicott thinks the appearances are listed in time order. He says "the Twelve" names the group, not the exact number present. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/15-5.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the appearances to the women are left out because they were evidence for the apostles rather than for the world. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/15-5.htm
- Calvin (Reformed) says "first to Peter" means first among the men, so it doesn't contradict Mark's statement that Jesus appeared first to Mary. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-5.html
- Guzik and Coffman both take the private appearance to Peter as restoration for the disciple who had denied Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-5.html
- Ray Stedman (quoted on Precept Austin) suggests Paul lists Peter first because a woman's testimony carried no legal weight then. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-15-commentary

**v. 6**
- Clarke (Methodist) thinks this appearance was probably in Galilee. Because most of the 500 were still alive, Paul could have been challenged if he were lying. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-corinthians-15.html

**v. 7**
- Benson (Methodist) says the Gospels don't mention this appearance. The church fathers identify this James as the Lord's brother. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-7.html

**v. 11**
- Clarke says all the apostles preached the same doctrine, including that Christ's resurrection is the pledge of ours. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-corinthians-15.html

**v. 12**
- Precept Austin thinks the Corinthians didn't deny Jesus' resurrection. More likely they denied that believers would be raised. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-15-commentary
- Guzik puts it this way: the Corinthians believed people live forever, but not in resurrected bodies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

**v. 13–16**
- Hodge (Reformed) asks why someone couldn't accept Christ's resurrection while denying a general one. His answer: "Because the thing denied was that the dead could rise." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hdg/1-corinthians-15.html
- On v. 15, both Hodge and Guzik say the apostles would be deliberate liars, because they claimed to have seen and touched the risen Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hdg/1-corinthians-15.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

**v. 17**
- Clarke says that if Christ wasn't raised, it would suggest he was justly put to death, so no atonement was made and people stay under sin's guilt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-corinthians-15.html

**v. 18**
- Matthew Henry says the Corinthian deniers seem to have thought death destroyed the whole person. Otherwise Paul could not argue that the Christian dead were lost. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm

**v. 19**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) say Christians face persecution that others escape. All hope of salvation, even for the soul, depends on Christ's resurrection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm

**v. 20**
- JFB note that the firstfruits offering was made on the day after the Passover Sabbath, the same day Christ rose. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm
- Hodge says Christ rose as a representative, the pledge for all who will ever sleep in Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hdg/1-corinthians-15.html
- Guzik says others were brought back to life before Jesus, but he was the first actually resurrected. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/firstfruits-of-the-resurrection/

**v. 21**
- Guzik says Adam and Christ are the two "heads" of humanity. Christ brings resurrection to everyone under his headship. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/weekly-devotionals/firstfruits-of-the-resurrection/

**v. 22: who are the "all"? (a real difference)**
- Matthew Henry: it does not follow that everyone without exception rises in this sense. Those who rise in Christ's sense rise through his merit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm
- Hodge: Christ secures life for all who are in him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hdg/1-corinthians-15.html
- JFB take a broader view. Everyone will rise because all humanity is united with Christ by nature. Believers rise to life because of their personal union with him. JFB also warn against concluding that all will be saved. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm
- Precept Austin says the resurrection here is the "first resurrection," which only believers share. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-corinthians-15-commentary
- The Bible Hub study note says Christ's redemption is available to all, received by faith. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/15-22.htm

**v. 23**
- Hodge: Christ rose first, and his people rise when he comes the second time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hdg/1-corinthians-15.html
- JFB: the godly rise as a separate group, and "the end" brings the resurrection of the rest. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm

**v. 24–26: the millennium (a major difference)**
- **Overview:** The Gospel Coalition says premillennialists cite vv. 20–28 for an in-between kingdom stage. Amillennialists and postmillennialists apply the passage to the church age or the final state. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/views-of-the-millennium/
- **Dispensational premillennial view:**
  - Constable says "the end" comes more than 1,000 years after the Rapture, when Christ hands over his earthly millennial reign. Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) agrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-24.html
  - J. Vernon McGee reads the passage the same way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mcgee_j_vernon/eBooks/millennium.cfm
  - Precept Austin says Christ rules through the millennium until the Great White Throne judgment, then places his kingdom under the Father. https://www.preceptaustin.org/revelation-topics-millennium
- **Historic premillennial view:** Robert Culver (on Monergism) says vv. 20–24 show that all will rise, but not at one time. A period of unrevealed length comes between. https://www.monergism.com/millennium
- **Amillennial view:**
  - Coffman says the Second Coming ends Christ's reign rather than starting it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-24.html
  - Another commentary on the same page notes that v. 25 uses the present tense, so Jesus is reigning now. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-24.html
  - Bob Utley (bible.org) says the text is about resurrection, not the millennium. He says death was defeated at the empty tomb. https://bible.org/seriespage/1-corinthians-15
- **Gill (Baptist)** sees a thousand-year reign on the new earth. He insists Christ does not stop reigning when he hands over the kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-24.html
- **v. 26:** JFB say death is abolished for believers above all, but even unbelievers are freed from death by the general resurrection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm

**v. 27**
- Guzik says this shows the Son will never be above the Father. The Father–Son relationship is eternal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/

**v. 28: how the Son is "subject"**
- **Ligonier (Reformed):** The subjection comes only as a result of the incarnation. As God, the Son is equal in authority. Ligonier cites Augustine on this. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/subjecting-all-things-to-christ
- **Poole and Barnes:** The subjection doesn't make the Son unequal. It means Christ hands over his kingdom as Mediator. Barnes says this has been the common reading of every age. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/15-28.htm
- **Guzik:** The Son's submission reflects the ordering of the Godhead, not inferiority. Father and Son relate as Father and Son forever. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-15/
- **GotQuestions:** In practice Jesus stays in eternal submission, while being equal in being. https://www.gotquestions.org/all-in-all.html
- **Gill:** He rejects both the Sabellian and the Arian readings. He takes the subjection as Christ, as man, giving account of his office as Mediator. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-28.html
- **Meyer (biblehub):** He argues that older interpreters imported doctrine so Paul wouldn't seem to teach an end to Christ's rule, which Meyer thinks Paul plainly does teach. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/15-28.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock (Challoner) says the Son is subject in his human nature, and the whole mystical body will be fully subject to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-28.html

**v. 29: "baptized for the dead"**
- **Proxy baptism:** The Pulpit Commentary says the verse can only mean an unwarranted practice of baptism by proxy, which Paul mentions without approving. Alford, quoted by JFB, holds a similar view. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/15-29.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Cr/1Cr_015.cfm
- **Bible Hub Q&A:** Proxy baptism was held by the Marcionites and is practised by Latter-day Saints today. The page prefers "because of the dead": converts moved to faith by believers who died in hope. It cites Chrysostom for this reading. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_baptized_for_the_dead.htm
- **GotQuestions:** It rules out salvation by proxy. It offers three readings: baptism in hope of resurrection (Barnes), filling the places of martyrs, or being won by the witness of the dead. https://www.gotquestions.org/baptism-dead.html ; https://www.gotquestions.org/baptized-for-the-dead.html
- **Calvin (Reformed):** It refers to people baptized when they had given up hope of living and were close to death. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom40/calcom40.i.iv.html
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Either baptized in hope of blessings after death, or stepping into the places of those who fell, like soldiers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-29.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** Baptism pictures death and resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-29.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** He leans toward a figurative "baptism" of suffering, but also says immersion pictures resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/15-29.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-29.html
- **Luther:** The Pulpit Commentary reports he read it as "over the graves of" the dead. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/15-29.htm
- **Catholic:** Haydock gives Chrysostom's reading (baptized professing belief in the resurrection) and another: people asking for baptism when in danger of death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/15-29.html
